title: Telling What Happened
overview: Until now everything you have said has been about the present or the future. This unit opens the past, and it is the single largest addition in Level 1: one ending, one list of irregulars worth memorising, and one rule about questions and negatives that removes half the work. It ends with an incident report and a witness statement about the same event, because the difference between what happened and what somebody remembers is where careful reading earns its keep.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns.
Open Patterns. Cards 1 and 2 are one pattern in two halves — do both together.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a report and a statement about one event.
Do the Practice. Practice 3 is the one that saves you the most work.
Record yourself telling what happened, twice.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
This is the biggest unit in Level 1, because it opens the past, and almost everything you want to say about your own life is in the past.
The good news arrives early: English has one past tense form for everybody. No he, she or it change. Not one.
I worked. You worked. She worked. They worked. All identical.
Compare that with the present simple, where you had to remember the -s in Unit 3. The past simple has nothing of the kind. Once you have the form, it works for every person.
First pattern: regular verbs. Add -ed.
Work becomes worked. Start becomes started. Finish becomes finished.
Three spelling rules, and they are the same three you already know from other endings.
If the verb ends in e, just add -d. Live becomes lived. Arrive becomes arrived.
If it ends in consonant plus y, change to i and add -ed. Study becomes studied. Try becomes tried.
And short verbs ending in one vowel plus one consonant double the last letter. Stop becomes stopped. Plan becomes planned.
Now pronunciation, because this surprises people. The -ed ending has three different sounds and none of them is a separate syllable except one.
After most sounds it is a t sound: worked, finished, stopped.
After voiced sounds it is a d sound: lived, arrived, opened.
And only after t or d does it become an extra syllable: started, wanted, needed. Star-ted. Wan-ted.
You do not need to memorise which is which. You need to know that started has two syllables and worked has one, because learners often add a syllable to all of them and it makes speech hard to follow.
Second pattern: irregular verbs. These do not take -ed and each one must be learned separately.
There are a lot of them and that sounds discouraging, so let me be precise about the actual size of the problem. There are about a hundred irregular verbs in common use. But the twenty most common cover the great majority of what you will actually say, and you already know several of them without realising.
Go becomes went. Be becomes was and were. Have becomes had. Do becomes did. Say becomes said. See becomes saw. Come becomes came. Give becomes gave. Take becomes took. Get becomes got. Know becomes knew. Think becomes thought. Tell becomes told. Find becomes found. Feel becomes felt. Hear becomes heard. Leave becomes left. Lose becomes lost. Make becomes made. Put stays put.
That is twenty and it is worth learning as a list, out loud, in pairs. Go went, see saw, come came. The pairs stick better than the single forms.
Be is the one that behaves differently, because it has two past forms. I was, he was, she was. You were, we were, they were. That is the only English verb that still changes for person in the past, and it is the most common verb in the language, so it is worth getting right early.
Third pattern: questions and negatives. This is where the work disappears.
To make a question or a negative in the past, you use did, and then the verb goes back to its plain form.
Did you go? Not did you went.
I did not go. Not I did not went.
Read that again, because it is the most useful rule in this unit. Once did is in the sentence, it carries the past, and the main verb has nothing left to do. So all your irregular verbs — went, saw, came, took — disappear in questions and negatives. You only need them in positive statements.
That halves the memorising. You need went for I went, and you never need it again for did you go or I did not go.
The contraction of did not is didn't.
And the exception, which is be: was and were do not use did at all. Were you there? I was not there. Be makes its own questions and negatives, exactly as it does in the present.
Fourth pattern: the past time markers. Two of them, and they work differently.
Ago comes after a period of time and means counting back from now. Two weeks ago. Three years ago. Ten minutes ago.
Last comes before a period and means the most recent one. Last week. Last month. Last year.
The error people make is putting them the wrong way round: ago two weeks, or week last. The order is fixed. A period then ago. Last then a period.
And one thing worth knowing: last night is correct, but yesterday night is not. Yesterday takes morning, afternoon and evening — yesterday morning, yesterday afternoon, yesterday evening — but for the night before, English says last night. There is no reason for it. It is just what is said.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: To move or travel to a place. Past: went.
words.example: I went to the office at eight.
practice: I went to the office at eight.
I did not go in the end.
words.starter: I went to the office at
words.tutor: Say go went five times, then use went in a sentence about yesterday.

words.meaning: To notice with your eyes. Past: saw.
practice: She saw him at the station.
We saw each other last week.
words.tutor: Say see saw five times. Notice saw sounds nothing like see.

words.meaning: To move towards the speaker or a place. Past: came.
words.example: She came in at about ten.
practice: She came in at about ten.
He came back an hour later.
words.tutor: Say come came five times. Then say did he come, with the plain form.

words.meaning: To hand something to somebody. Past: gave.
practice: I gave it back the next day.
Did they give you a receipt?
words.tutor: Say give gave five times. Then say did they give, with the plain form.

words.meaning: To give information to somebody in words. Past: told.
practice: She told me it was cancelled.
He told the manager the next morning.
words.tutor: Notice tell takes a person: tell me, told them. Say told me and told them.

words.meaning: To discover something, often by looking. Past: found.
words.example: I found it under the seat.
practice: I found it under the seat.
She found it very difficult at first.
words.tutor: Say find found five times. Then ask did you find, with the plain form.

words.meaning: To speak words. Past: said, which sounds like sed.
practice: They said it would take a week.
words.tutor: Said does not rhyme with paid. It sounds like sed. Say it five times.

words.meaning: To have information in your mind. Past: knew.
practice: I did not know his name.
words.tutor: The k in know and knew is silent. Say know knew five times.

words.meaning: To have an opinion or use your mind. Past: thought.
practice: She thought about it for a week.
We thought the shop was open.
I did not think it would rain.
words.tutor: Thought is one syllable and the gh is silent. Say think thought five times.

words.meaning: To experience an emotion or a physical sensation. Past: felt.
words.example: I felt ill in the afternoon.
practice: I felt ill in the afternoon.
She felt much better the next day.
I felt very tired after the shift.
He did not feel well enough to work.
words.tutor: Say feel felt five times. Then ask how did you feel, with the plain form.

words.meaning: To notice a sound. Past: heard, which rhymes with word.
practice: I heard about it from a colleague.
I did not hear anything at all.
words.tutor: Heard rhymes with word, not with beard. Say hear heard five times.

words.meaning: To no longer have something, or not to know where it is. Past: lost.
words.example: I lost my key on the way home.
practice: I lost my key on the way home.
We lost an hour because of the delay.
He lost his job in March.
words.starter: I lost my key on the way
words.tutor: Say lose lost five times. Notice lose has one o sound and lost has another.

words.meaning: To take place, especially without being planned.
practice: It happened at about four o'clock.
words.tutor: Happen is regular: happened. Notice the p is not doubled.

words.meaning: Something bad that happens without anyone intending it.
words.example: There was an accident on the coast road.
practice: There was an accident on the coast road.
It was an accident — nobody did it deliberately.
The accident happened at about six.
Was anybody hurt in the accident?
There have been three accidents here.
words.starter: There was an accident on the
words.tutor: Say by accident, meaning not deliberately. Use it in one sentence.

words.meaning: Something done wrongly, usually without meaning to.
words.example: It was my mistake and I said so.
practice: It was my mistake and I said so.
I made a mistake with the order.
It was a mistake to leave so late.
She found the mistake straight away.
words.starter: It was my mistake and I
words.tutor: English says make a mistake, not do a mistake. Say make a mistake three times.

words.meaning: Something difficult that needs to be dealt with.
words.example: There was a problem with the delivery.
practice: There was a problem with the delivery.
The problem was the weather, not the driver.
words.starter: There was a problem with the
words.tutor: Notice problem takes with: a problem with something. Say it twice.

words.meaning: Why something happened.
practice: What was the reason for the delay?
There is a good reason for it.
words.tutor: Say the reason for something, and the reason why. Both are used.

words.meaning: What happens because of something else.
words.example: As a result, the road was closed.
practice: As a result, the road was closed.
The result was a two-hour delay.
As a result of the storm, the ferry was cancelled.
The result was better than we expected.
words.starter: As a result, the road was
words.tutor: As a result does the same job as so from Unit 13, but in more formal writing.

words.meaning: Quickly and without warning.
practice: Suddenly there was a loud noise.
words.tutor: Suddenly usually starts a sentence in a story. Use it to begin one.

words.meaning: At once, with no delay.
practice: She left immediately after the meeting.
I immediately knew something was wrong.
words.tutor: Say immediately and at once. They mean the same thing.

words.meaning: After a long time, or as the last thing.
practice: Finally, I would like to thank everybody.
It finally stopped raining at six.
words.tutor: Finally can mean at last, or it can introduce your last point. Use it both ways.

words.meaning: Fortunately; it is good that this happened.
practice: Luckily the shop was still open.
Luckily it stopped before we left.
words.tutor: Luckily comments on the whole sentence. Start a sentence with it.

words.meaning: It is bad that this happened.
words.example: Unfortunately the last bus had gone.
practice: Unfortunately the last bus had gone.
words.tutor: Unfortunately is the opposite of luckily. Say a sentence with each.

words.meaning: After that; later.
words.tutor: Say afterwards and after that. They do the same job in a story.

words.meaning: Counting back from now. It comes after the period of time.
words.example: It happened about two weeks ago.
practice: It happened about two weeks ago.
I started this job three months ago.
words.tutor: The period comes first, then ago. Say two weeks ago, never ago two weeks.

words.meaning: The day before today.
words.tutor: Yesterday takes morning, afternoon and evening — but for night, English says last night.

words.meaning: Not long ago.
practice: Recently the weather has been very wet.
words.tutor: Recently is vaguer than ago. Say one sentence with each.

words.meaning: One time; or at some point in the past.
practice: It happened once, about a year ago.
Once, the road was closed for a week.
I have only done that once.
words.tutor: Once means one time, and it also means at some time in the past. Use both.

words.meaning: Before the time being talked about.
words.example: I telephoned earlier but there was no answer.
practice: I telephoned earlier but there was no answer.
It happened earlier in the week.
I saw him earlier this morning.
Earlier, the road had been open.
words.starter: I telephoned earlier but there was no
words.tutor: Earlier is the comparative of early, from Unit 4, used as a time word.

readings.title: Twenty Verbs, Not a Hundred
readings.passage:
Irregular verbs have a reputation for being the hardest thing in English, and the reputation is mostly undeserved. The problem is real but it is much smaller than it looks.
There are about a hundred irregular verbs in common use. That is the number that frightens people. But the twenty most common cover the great majority of everything you will actually say, and the reason is simple: the most common verbs in any language are the oldest, and the oldest ones are the irregular ones. Go, be, have, do, say, see, come, give, take, get. Those ten alone appear in nearly every conversation you will have.
So the sensible order is: learn twenty properly, and meet the rest as they arrive.
There are two things that make the twenty stick.
Learn them in pairs, out loud. Go went, see saw, come came, give gave. The pair is one item of memory; the two forms separately are two. Saying them aloud matters more than reading them, because the irregular part is usually a sound rather than a spelling.
And learn them in sentences you would actually say. I went to work. I saw her yesterday. Nobody told me. A verb learned inside a sentence you use is far more durable than one learned in a list, because you will meet it again by accident.
The other piece of good news is in Pattern 3. Irregular forms only appear in positive statements. As soon as there is a question or a negative, did takes over and the verb goes back to its plain form. So you need went for I went, and never again for did you go or I didn't go.
That means the twenty forms have half the work you thought they did.

readings.title: Two People, One Event
readings.passage:
When something happens and two people describe it, the accounts will differ. That is normal, and it is not usually because somebody is lying.
People notice different things. Somebody watching the road notices the vehicle; somebody watching the pavement notices the person. Both accounts are honest and neither is complete.
People also fill gaps without knowing they have done it. Memory does not store an event like a recording. It stores fragments and rebuilds the rest each time you recall it, using what seems reasonable. The rebuilt parts feel exactly as certain as the remembered parts, which is why confidence is a poor guide to accuracy.
And time is the least reliable thing of all. Ask two witnesses how long something lasted and the answers can differ by a factor of five. Ask what time it happened and you will often get an approximation stated as a fact.
So when you read two accounts, there are three useful questions.
What do both accounts agree on? That is the most solid ground available.
Where do they differ, and is the difference about a fact or about an interpretation? He was driving too fast is an interpretation. He was going about fifty is a claim about a fact.
And what does each account not mention? A witness statement that does not mention the weather may mean the weather was unremarkable, or may mean the witness never looked. Absence is ambiguous, and it is worth noticing without over-reading it.
This matters beyond accidents. Any time you have two versions of one event — two colleagues describing a meeting, two documents describing the same delay — the same three questions apply.

readings.title: The Report, and What the Witness Said
readings.setting: A workplace incident report, and a statement written by somebody who saw it.
readings.passage:
INCIDENT REPORT
  Northfield Warehouse

  DATE      Tuesday 14 March
  TIME      15:40 (approx)
  LOCATION  Loading bay 2

  WHAT HAPPENED
  A stack of boxes fell from a trolley.
  One employee stepped back and was not
  struck. No injuries.

  ACTION TAKEN
  Area cleared 15:45. Boxes restacked.
  Supervisor informed 16:10.

  CAUSE
  Trolley was loaded above the marked
  line.

  REPORTED BY  D. Okonkwo, Supervisor
  COMPLETED    17:20 same day

-----------------------------------------

  WITNESS STATEMENT

  I was working in bay 2 on Tuesday
  afternoon. I think it was about half
  past three.

  I heard a noise behind me and turned
  round. The boxes were already on the
  floor, so I did not see them fall.

  Sara was standing about two metres
  away. She stepped back very quickly.
  Nothing hit her.

  The trolley looked very full to me but
  I did not measure it.

  I told the supervisor straight away. I
  think that was about twenty minutes
  later, because I finished the pallet
  I was on first.

  Signed: J. Marsh

comprehension.q: Why does the text say the irregular verb problem is smaller than it looks?
comprehension.a: Because the twenty most common irregulars cover the great majority of what you will actually say, even though about a hundred exist.
comprehension.why: The frightening number and the useful number are different, and only the useful one needs learning first.

comprehension.q: Why are the most common verbs the irregular ones?
comprehension.a: Because the most common verbs in a language are the oldest, and the oldest ones are the irregular ones.
comprehension.why: This is a fact about how languages change, and it explains why the difficulty is concentrated exactly where you cannot avoid it.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say to learn them in pairs and out loud?
comprehension.a: A pair is one item of memory rather than two, and saying them aloud matters because the irregular part is usually a sound rather than a spelling.
comprehension.why: Both halves of the advice are practical. Reading go and went silently does not teach you that went sounds nothing like go.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say two honest accounts of one event will still differ?
comprehension.a: Because people notice different things — somebody watching the road notices the vehicle, somebody watching the pavement notices the person.
comprehension.why: Difference is the normal case, not evidence of dishonesty. That framing is what makes the rest of the reading usable.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say confidence is a poor guide to accuracy?
comprehension.a: Because memory rebuilds the missing parts of an event each time it is recalled, and the rebuilt parts feel exactly as certain as the remembered ones.
comprehension.why: This is the least intuitive point in the reading and the most useful. A confident witness and an accurate one are not the same thing.

comprehension.q: What three questions does the text give for reading two accounts?
comprehension.a: What do both agree on, where do they differ and is that difference about a fact or an interpretation, and what does each not mention.
comprehension.why: The three work in order, from the most solid ground to the most ambiguous, and they apply well beyond accidents.

comprehension.q: What time did the incident happen, according to each document?
comprehension.a: The report says 15:40 approximately. The witness thinks it was about half past three. They differ by about ten minutes, and both are hedged.
comprehension.why: Neither states a time flatly, which is appropriate. Reading 2 warns that times are the least reliable detail, and both writers here behave accordingly.

comprehension.q: The report says a stack of boxes fell from a trolley. Did the witness see that?
comprehension.a: No. The witness heard a noise, turned round, and the boxes were already on the floor — so the falling itself was not witnessed.
comprehension.why: This is the most important gap in the document. The report states the event as fact; the only account of it comes from somebody who did not see it happen.

comprehension.q: The report gives the cause as the trolley being loaded above the marked line. How well does the witness support that?
comprehension.a: Only partly. The witness says the trolley looked very full but adds that they did not measure it — so it supports the report as an impression, not as evidence.
comprehension.why: Looked very full is an interpretation; above the marked line is a claim about a fact. Distinguishing those two is exactly the second question in Reading 2.

comprehension.q: The report says the supervisor was informed at 16:10. Does the witness statement agree?
comprehension.a: Roughly. The witness says they told the supervisor straight away, then says it was about twenty minutes later because they finished a pallet first.
comprehension.why: Straight away and twenty minutes later contradict each other inside one statement, and the witness supplies the reason without seeming to notice. The report's 16:10 fits the twenty minutes, not the straight away.

grammar.title: Past simple: regular -ed
grammar.explanation: One ending, and it is the same for every person. No he, she or it change anywhere in the past simple — which makes it simpler than the present simple you learned in Unit 5.
grammar.rule:
ADD -ED. Same for everybody.
  I worked.    You worked.
  She worked.  They worked.

THREE SPELLING RULES — all familiar
  ends in e        -> add -d
     live -> lived,  arrive -> arrived
  consonant + y    -> y becomes i
     study -> studied,  try -> tried
  short, one vowel + one consonant -> double
     stop -> stopped,  plan -> planned

PRONUNCIATION — three sounds, one syllable rule
  t sound:  worked, finished, stopped
  d sound:  lived, arrived, opened
  EXTRA SYLLABLE only after t or d:
     started (star-ted), wanted, needed

  worked = 1 syllable.  started = 2.
grammar.workedExample:
Put stop into the past.
1. Is it regular? Yes — it is not on the irregular list.
2. Check the spelling rules. It is short, and it ends in one vowel plus one consonant, so the last letter doubles.
3. Result: stopped.
4. Say it aloud. It ends in p, so the ending is a t sound and there is no extra syllable. Stopped, one syllable.
Now try start.
1. Regular. 2. No spelling change — just add -ed: started.
3. But it ends in t, so this is the one case where the ending becomes an extra syllable: star-ted, two syllables.
That is the whole pattern. The spelling has three rules; the pronunciation has one rule worth knowing, which is that only t and d add a syllable.
grammar.mistake: Adding a syllable to every -ed verb — saying work-ed and stop-ped. Only verbs already ending in t or d do this. The other error is forgetting the doubling in short verbs: stoped, planed. And a third, which is really a Unit 5 habit: adding -s in the past. She workeds does not exist; nothing changes for person in the past simple.
grammar.tip: One form for everybody. Only t and d add a syllable.
grammar.practice:
Write the past simple, then write 1 or 2 for the number of syllables.
1. work
2. start
3. live
4. study
5. stop
6. want
7. finish
8. arrive
grammar.answers:
1. worked — 1
2. started — 2
3. lived — 1
4. studied — 2 (stu-died)
5. stopped — 1
6. wanted — 2
7. finished — 2 (fin-ished, but the -ed itself adds nothing)
8. arrived — 2 (ar-rived, and again the -ed adds nothing)
The ones where the -ed itself is an extra syllable are 2 and 6 only — started and wanted — because those are the two ending in t.
Check your spellings: studied changed y to i, stopped doubled the p, and lived and arrived only added -d.

grammar.title: The twenty irregular verbs that matter
grammar.explanation: These do not take -ed and each must be learned. About a hundred exist; these twenty cover the great majority of what you will say. Learn them in pairs, aloud.
grammar.rule:
go      went        know    knew
be      was/were    think   thought
have    had         tell    told
do      did         find    found
say     said        feel    felt
see     saw         hear    heard
come    came        leave   left
give    gave        lose    lost
take    took        make    made
get     got         put     put

BE IS THE ODD ONE — two past forms:
  I was,  he was,  she was
  you were, we were, they were

  It is the only English verb that still
  changes for person in the past.

SOUNDS TO WATCH:
  said   sounds like sed, not paid
  heard  rhymes with word, not beard
grammar.workedExample:
Say that you travelled to the office yesterday.
1. The verb is go. Is it regular? No — it is on the list.
2. The past form is went. There is no rule; it is memorised.
3. Result: I went to the office yesterday.
Now the same verb for somebody else: She went to the office. Identical. Nothing changes for person.
Now be, which is the exception: I was late. They were late. Two forms, and which one depends on the person.
The pair drill is what makes these stick: go went, see saw, come came, give gave, take took. Say the pair, not the single form, because you will need to move between them constantly.
grammar.mistake: Adding -ed to an irregular verb — goed, seed, taked. This is the most common past-tense error and it is a sign of the rule being applied correctly to the wrong verb, which is progress rather than failure. The other error is with be: they was late. Was is for I, he, she and it; were is for you, we and they.
grammar.tip: Learn them in pairs, aloud. Be is the only one that changes for person.
grammar.practice:
Write the past simple.
1. I ____ (go) to the office at eight.
2. She ____ (see) it happen.
3. Nobody ____ (tell) me.
4. I ____ (think) it was Thursday.
5. They ____ (be) late.
6. I ____ (be) late.
7. He ____ (lose) his key.
8. We ____ (have) a problem with the delivery.
grammar.answers:
1. went  2. saw  3. told  4. thought  5. were  6. was  7. lost  8. had
Numbers 5 and 6 are the same verb with two different forms, because be is the only English verb that still changes for person in the past. They were, I was.
If you wrote goed, seed or telled for 1, 2 or 3, that is the regular rule applied to an irregular verb — the rule is right and the verb is on the list. Say the pair aloud ten times: go went, see saw, tell told.

grammar.title: Past questions and negatives: did
grammar.explanation: This is where the work disappears. Once did is in the sentence, it carries the past, and the main verb goes back to its plain form — so all your irregular forms vanish from questions and negatives.
grammar.rule:
QUESTION:  did + person + PLAIN VERB
  Did you go?          NOT  Did you went?
  Did she see it?      NOT  Did she saw it?

NEGATIVE:  did not + PLAIN VERB
  I did not go.        NOT  I did not went.
  She didn't see it.

  did not -> didn't

WHY THIS HELPS:
  You need went only for  I went.
  You never need it for   did you go
                    or    I didn't go.

THE EXCEPTION — be uses no did at all:
  Were you there?      NOT  Did you be there?
  I was not there.     NOT  I did not was there.
grammar.workedExample:
Turn I went to the office into a question.
1. Questions in the past use did.
2. Once did is there, it carries the past — so the main verb loses its past form and goes back to plain.
3. Went becomes go again.
4. Result: Did you go to the office?
Now the negative: I did not go to the office. Same rule, same plain verb. Contracted: I didn't go.
Now the exception. I was late is be, and be never uses did. The question is Were you late? and the negative is I wasn't late. If you find yourself writing did you be, the verb is be and it makes its own questions.
The test: if did is in the sentence, no other word carries the past.
grammar.mistake: Putting the past on both verbs — did you went, I didn't saw. This is by far the most common error in this unit, and it happens because both halves feel like they should agree. They should not: did has already done the job. The other error is using did with be — did you be there, I didn't was there. Be makes its own questions and negatives, in the past exactly as in the present.
grammar.tip: If did is in the sentence, the main verb goes plain.
grammar.practice:
Write the question and the negative.
1. I went to the office.
2. She saw it happen.
3. They told me.
4. He lost his key.
5. I was late.
6. They were there.
grammar.answers:
1. Did you go to the office? / I didn't go to the office.
2. Did she see it happen? / She didn't see it happen.
3. Did they tell you? / They didn't tell me.
4. Did he lose his key? / He didn't lose his key.
5. Were you late? / I wasn't late.
6. Were they there? / They weren't there.
In 1 to 4 every irregular form disappeared: went became go, saw became see, told became tell, lost became lose. That is the rule doing its work, and it is why the twenty forms are half the job they look like.
Numbers 5 and 6 use no did at all, because the verb is be.

grammar.title: Ago and last
grammar.explanation: Two time markers for the past. They work in opposite directions and the word order is fixed for both.
grammar.rule:
AGO — counting back from now
  comes AFTER the period
     two weeks ago
     three years ago
     ten minutes ago

LAST — the most recent one
  comes BEFORE the period
     last week
     last month
     last year

THE ORDER IS FIXED:
  period + ago      NOT  ago two weeks
  last + period     NOT  week last

ONE ODDITY WORTH KNOWING:
  yesterday morning    correct
  yesterday afternoon  correct
  yesterday evening    correct
  yesterday night      WRONG
  last night           correct

  There is no reason. It is just what
  is said.
grammar.workedExample:
Say that something happened fourteen days before today.
1. You are counting back from now, so this is ago, not last.
2. Ago comes after the period.
3. Choose the period: two weeks.
4. Result: It happened two weeks ago.
Now say it happened in the most recent week rather than counting back.
1. The most recent one takes last.
2. Last comes before the period: last week.
3. Result: It happened last week.
Those two sentences point at slightly different things. Two weeks ago is a measured distance backwards. Last week is a named period. Both are correct English and they are not interchangeable.
grammar.mistake: Reversing the order — ago two weeks, or week last. The position is fixed for both words and swapping it is immediately noticeable. The other error is yesterday night, which does not exist in English; the night before today is last night, even though yesterday morning, afternoon and evening are all fine.
grammar.tip: Period then ago. Last then period.
grammar.practice:
Write the time expression.
1. Fourteen days before today, counting back.
2. The most recent week.
3. Ten minutes before now.
4. The most recent year.
5. The night before today.
6. The morning of the day before today.
grammar.answers:
1. two weeks ago
2. last week
3. ten minutes ago
4. last year
5. last night
6. yesterday morning
Numbers 5 and 6 are the pair worth checking. The night before today is last night, but the morning before today is yesterday morning. Yesterday night is not English.
In 1 and 3 the period came first. In 2 and 4 last came first. That order never varies.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — One syllable or two
speaking.instructions:
Say these eight past forms aloud and count the syllables on your fingers as you go.
worked, started, lived, studied, stopped, wanted, finished, needed
Record them.
Play back and check: only started, wanted and needed should have gained a syllable from the -ed. If worked came out as work-ed, say the four one-syllable ones ten more times.
This matters more than it sounds. Adding a syllable to every past verb makes speech noticeably harder to follow.
speaking.tutor: Say eight past forms and ask the tutor which ones have an extra syllable.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The pair drill
speaking.instructions:
Say all twenty pairs aloud, in order, twice.
go went, be was were, have had, do did, say said, see saw, come came, give gave, take took, get got, know knew, think thought, tell told, find found, feel felt, hear heard, leave left, lose lost, make made, put put
Record the second time through.
Then close the book and say as many pairs as you can from memory. Write down the ones you could not.
Those are your list. Say those aloud five times a day until they arrive without effort.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to give you the plain form and say the past form before it does.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Questions and negatives
speaking.instructions:
Take six sentences about yesterday, using irregular verbs.
Say each one three ways: the statement, the question, the negative.
I went to work. Did you go to work? I didn't go to work.
Record all eighteen.
Play back and listen for did you went or I didn't saw. If you hear either, that is the error this whole card exists to prevent — say those three sets again slowly.
speaking.tutor: Say six past statements and ask the tutor to turn each into a question and a negative.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — What happened yesterday
speaking.instructions:
Tell the story of yesterday, from waking up to going to bed.
Eight to ten sentences.
Use at least six irregular verbs and at least three regular ones.
Use at least two of the story adverbs: suddenly, immediately, finally, luckily, unfortunately, afterwards.
Record it.
Then listen back and count the irregular verbs you got wrong. That number is your practice list for tomorrow.
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor about yesterday and ask it to list any past forms you got wrong.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Ago and last
speaking.instructions:
Say twelve sentences about real events in your own past.
Six with ago — ten minutes ago, two weeks ago, three years ago.
Six with last — last night, last week, last month.
Record them.
Play back and check the order in every one: the period comes before ago, and last comes before the period. And check you said last night rather than yesterday night.
speaking.tutor: Say six sentences with ago and six with last, and ask the tutor to flag any wrong order.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the two accounts aloud
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the incident report aloud, then the witness statement.
Notice the difference in your own voice — the report states, the statement hedges.
Then say aloud, as though explaining to somebody: what both accounts agree on, and the one thing the report states as fact that nobody actually saw.
Then say what the witness contradicts inside their own statement, and why it matters.
Record the last two parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor both accounts and ask what it would want to check before signing the report.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A day, told properly
writing.prompt:
Write about one real day in your past — yesterday, or a day you remember.
Ten to fourteen sentences.
Use at least eight irregular verbs from the list and at least four regular ones.
Use at least three story adverbs: suddenly, immediately, finally, luckily, unfortunately, afterwards.
Use ago or last at least twice.
Then underline every irregular past form and check each one against the list.
writing.model:
Last Tuesday started badly. I woke up late because I did not hear the alarm, and I left the house about twenty minutes later than usual.
I went to the bus stop and waited. Unfortunately the bus did not come. I waited about fifteen minutes and then I saw on the sign that the route had changed the week before. Nobody told me, and I had not looked.
I walked to the station instead. It took twenty-five minutes and I got there at nine.
Suddenly, on the platform, I realised I had left my card at home. Luckily I found some cash in my coat, so I bought a ticket at the window.
I arrived at work at half past nine. My supervisor said nothing about it, which was kind of her. Afterwards I felt worse than if she had said something.
I checked the bus route that evening. It changed three weeks ago.
writing.criteria: At least eight irregular past forms, all correct and underlined; at least four regular -ed forms with correct spelling; at least three story adverbs; ago or last used at least twice with the right word order
writing.support: Write the day as a list of events first, in order, using plain verbs — wake, leave, go, wait, see. Then convert the list to past forms. Separating what happened from how to say it makes both easier.
writing.extension: Rewrite three of the sentences as questions and three as negatives. Every irregular form should disappear when you do.

writing.title: Writing 2 — An incident report and a statement
writing.prompt:
Invent one small incident — something that went wrong at work, on a journey, or in a shop.
Write two documents about it.
First a report: date, time, location, what happened, action taken, cause. Short, factual sentences.
Then a witness statement from somebody who saw part of it. First person, hedged where the witness is unsure.
The two must be about the same event and must not agree completely.
writing.model:
INCIDENT REPORT
DATE  Thursday 6 June
TIME  10:15 (approx)
LOCATION  Front counter
WHAT HAPPENED  A customer's bag was left at the counter and was not noticed for about an hour. It was returned to the owner the same day.
ACTION TAKEN  Bag placed in the office 11:20. Owner telephoned 11:35. Collected 16:00.
CAUSE  Counter was unattended between 10:15 and 11:00 because of a staff shortage.
REPORTED BY  A. Reyes, Assistant Manager

WITNESS STATEMENT
I was on the till on Thursday morning. I think the customer left at about a quarter past ten, but I did not look at the clock.
I saw the bag but I thought it belonged to the woman behind her, so I did not say anything.
I did not know the counter was unattended. I was there the whole time, but I was serving, so I was not really watching the counter itself.
I told the assistant manager when I went on my break. I think that was about eleven.
Signed: K. Devlin
writing.criteria: Report is factual with no hedging and includes all six headings; statement is first person and hedges at least three times; the two accounts differ on at least one point; the statement contains at least one thing the witness did not see or know
writing.support: Write the report first, then write the statement from inside one person's head — and let them be wrong about something. The whole exercise fails if the two accounts agree completely, because agreement is what real accounts almost never do.
writing.extension: Underline every hedge in the statement and every flat assertion in the report. The two lists should not overlap at all.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the report and the statement
writing.prompt:
Use the report and statement in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. What time did it happen, according to each document?
2. The report says the boxes fell from a trolley. Did the witness see that?
3. How well does the witness support the stated cause?
4. The report says the supervisor was informed at 16:10. Does the witness agree?
5. Name one thing both accounts agree on, and one thing neither mentions.
writing.model:
1. The report says 15:40 approximately and the witness thinks about half past three. They differ by roughly ten minutes, and both are hedged rather than stated flatly.
2. No. The witness heard a noise, turned round, and the boxes were already on the floor, so nobody in these documents actually saw them fall.
3. Only partly. The witness says the trolley looked very full but adds that they did not measure it. That supports the cause as an impression, not as evidence — looked very full is an interpretation, above the marked line is a claim about a fact.
4. Roughly, but the witness contradicts themselves. They say they told the supervisor straight away and then say it was about twenty minutes later because they finished a pallet first. The report's 16:10 fits the twenty minutes rather than the straight away.
5. Both agree that Sara stepped back and was not struck. Neither mentions who was pushing the trolley.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 2 identifies that the central event was unwitnessed; answer 3 distinguishes interpretation from fact; answer 4 identifies the internal contradiction; answer 5 names a genuine shared point and a genuine absence
writing.support: Read both documents and mark every hedge — approximately, I think, looked, about. The report has one and the statement has five, and that difference is most of what these two documents are showing you.
writing.extension: Write the two questions you would ask the witness to resolve the contradiction in answer 4.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the ten mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I goed to the office at eight.
2. Did you went yesterday?
3. I didn't saw anything.
4. She workeds here last year.
5. It happened ago two weeks.
6. I saw her yesterday night.
7. They was late.
8. Did you be there?
9. I stoped at the crossing.
10. She studyed for three years.
writing.model:
1. I went to the office at eight. (Pattern 2 — go is irregular, so no -ed)
2. Did you go yesterday? (Pattern 3 — after did, the verb goes plain)
3. I didn't see anything. (Pattern 3 — after didn't, the verb goes plain)
4. She worked here last year. (Pattern 1 — nothing changes for person in the past simple)
5. It happened two weeks ago. (Pattern 4 — the period comes before ago)
6. I saw her last night. (Pattern 4 — yesterday night does not exist in English)
7. They were late. (Pattern 2 — be is the only verb that changes for person in the past)
8. Were you there? (Pattern 3 — be never uses did)
9. I stopped at the crossing. (Pattern 1 — short verbs double the last letter)
10. She studied for three years. (Pattern 1 — consonant plus y changes to i)
writing.criteria: All ten corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; numbers 2, 3 and 8 all return a verb to its plain form or remove did entirely
writing.support: Numbers 2, 3 and 8 are one rule in three disguises. In 2 and 3 did is doing its job and the second verb should not repeat the past. In 8 the verb is be, which never uses did at all.
writing.extension: Numbers 1 and 4 are opposite errors — an irregular verb given -ed, and a regular verb given a person ending. Write two more of each.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Regular past forms
activities.instructions:
Write the past simple, then write 1 or 2 for the number of syllables in the whole word.
1. work
2. start
3. live
4. study
5. stop
6. want
7. finish
8. arrive
9. plan
10. need
11. try
12. open
activities.answers:
1. worked — 1
2. started — 2
3. lived — 1
4. studied — 2
5. stopped — 1
6. wanted — 2
7. finished — 2
8. arrived — 2
9. planned — 1
10. needed — 2
11. tried — 1
12. opened — 2
The verbs where the -ed itself adds a syllable are 2, 6 and 10 — started, wanted, needed — and all three already ended in t or d. Everywhere else the -ed adds a sound but not a syllable.
Spelling to check: stopped and planned doubled the last letter; studied and tried changed y to i; lived and arrived only added -d.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Irregular past forms
activities.instructions:
Write the past simple.
1. I ____ (go) to the office at eight.
2. She ____ (see) it happen.
3. Nobody ____ (tell) me.
4. I ____ (think) it was Thursday.
5. They ____ (be) late.
6. I ____ (be) late.
7. He ____ (lose) his key.
8. We ____ (have) a problem.
9. She ____ (give) me the form.
10. I ____ (hear) a noise outside.
11. He ____ (come) back an hour later.
12. I ____ (find) it under the seat.
activities.answers:
1. went  2. saw  3. told  4. thought  5. were  6. was  7. lost  8. had  9. gave  10. heard  11. came  12. found
Numbers 5 and 6 are the same verb with two forms. Be is the only English verb that still changes for person in the past: I was, they were.
If you wrote goed, seed, telled or finded anywhere, that is the regular rule applied to an irregular verb. The rule is correct; the verb is on the list. Say those pairs aloud ten times.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Questions and negatives
activities.instructions:
Write the question and the negative for each statement.
1. I went to the office.
2. She saw it happen.
3. They told me.
4. He lost his key.
5. I was late.
6. They were there.
7. She gave me the form.
8. We had a problem.
9. I heard the announcement.
10. He came back.
11. I found it.
12. She knew about it.
activities.answers:
1. Did you go to the office? / I didn't go to the office.
2. Did she see it happen? / She didn't see it happen.
3. Did they tell you? / They didn't tell me.
4. Did he lose his key? / He didn't lose his key.
5. Were you late? / I wasn't late.
6. Were they there? / They weren't there.
7. Did she give you the form? / She didn't give me the form.
8. Did you have a problem? / We didn't have a problem.
9. Did you hear the announcement? / I didn't hear the announcement.
10. Did he come back? / He didn't come back.
11. Did you find it? / I didn't find it.
12. Did she know about it? / She didn't know about it.
Count how many irregular past forms survived into your answers. It should be none, except in 5 and 6 where the verb is be and did is not used at all.
That is the point of this exercise. Ten irregular forms went into it and none came out, because did carries the past on its own.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Ago or last?
activities.instructions:
Write the time expression.
1. Fourteen days before today, counting back.
2. The most recent week.
3. Ten minutes before now.
4. The most recent year.
5. The night before today.
6. The morning of the day before today.
7. Three years before now.
8. The most recent month.
9. The evening of the day before today.
10. About an hour before now.
activities.answers:
1. two weeks ago  2. last week  3. ten minutes ago  4. last year  5. last night  6. yesterday morning  7. three years ago  8. last month  9. yesterday evening  10. about an hour ago
Numbers 5, 6 and 9 are the set worth checking together. Yesterday takes morning, afternoon and evening — but not night. The night before today is last night, and there is no reason for it.
In every ago answer the period came first. In every last answer last came first. Neither order ever varies.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Your own twenty
activities.instructions:
Write the twenty irregular pairs from memory, without looking.
Then check them against the list in Pattern 2.
Circle every one you got wrong or could not remember.
Write each circled verb inside a sentence about your own life — not a made-up sentence, a real one.
Say those sentences aloud every day this week.
activities.answers:
No key beyond the list in Pattern 2 — the point is which ones you missed.
What most people find: between four and eight are missing on the first attempt, and they are usually the same ones — thought, heard, found, felt, knew. The ones with a vowel change and no obvious pattern are harder than the ones that look like the present.
The second finding is that a verb written into a real sentence about your own life stays learned much longer than one drilled from a list. That is why this task asks for real sentences and not invented ones — you will meet your own sentence again by accident, and the list you will not.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Ask somebody what happened
activities.instructions:
This week, ask somebody about something that happened to them — a journey, a day at work, a weekend.
Ask at least four past questions with did.
Write down: the four questions you asked, and one thing you learned that you would not have known.
Then note whether you said did you went at any point. Most people do, at least once.
activities.answers:
No key.
What most people find: the did rule is secure in writing and slips in speech, because the past feels like it should be marked twice. Catching yourself doing it is the fix — nobody corrects this error away by being told about it once.
The second finding is that four questions is enough to get a real story. Past questions are the most productive questions in English for keeping a conversation going, because everybody has a yesterday and almost nobody minds being asked about it.

options: I go to the office yesterday.
I did went to the office.
quizzes.why: Go is irregular, so it does not take -ed. And did is not used in a positive statement — only in questions and negatives.
Once did is in the sentence it carries the past, so the main verb goes back to its plain form. This is the most common error in the unit.

quizzes.q: Which past form has an extra syllable from the -ed?
quizzes.why: Only verbs already ending in t or d gain a syllable. Start ends in t, so started is star-ted. The other three are one syllable each.
The period of time comes first and ago comes after it. Last works the other way round: last week, not week last.
Be is the only English verb that still changes for person in the past. Was is for I, he, she and it; were is for you, we and they.
After didn't the verb goes plain. The irregular form saw is needed only in a positive statement.

quizzes.q: How do you make a past question with be?
quizzes.why: Be never uses did, in the past exactly as in the present. It makes its own questions and negatives.

quizzes.q: What is the past simple of study?
quizzes.why: Consonant plus y changes to i before -ed. The same change happens in the superlative — the easiest, the busiest — from Unit 12.

options: I saw her the last night.
quizzes.why: Yesterday takes morning, afternoon and evening, but not night. The night before today is last night, and there is no reason for it.

quizzes.q: Which sentence has the person ending wrongly added?
quizzes.why: Nothing changes for person in the past simple — the form is identical for I, you, he, she, we and they. That makes it simpler than the present simple.

quizzes.q: Reading 1 says the twenty most common irregular verbs are worth learning first. Why are the commonest verbs irregular?
options: They are borrowed from other languages
Because the commonest verbs are the oldest, and the oldest are irregular
quizzes.a: Because the commonest verbs are the oldest, and the oldest are irregular
quizzes.why: This is a fact about how languages change, and it explains why the difficulty sits exactly where you cannot avoid it.

quizzes.q: The witness says the trolley looked very full but that they did not measure it. What kind of claim is that?
options: An interpretation rather than a fact
quizzes.a: An interpretation rather than a fact
quizzes.why: Looked very full is what somebody judged; above the marked line is a claim about a fact. Telling those apart is the second of the three questions in Reading 2.

teacherNotes.note: Four pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key. Practice 3 is the diagnostic and its answer key ends by asking the learner to count how many irregular forms survived into their answers — the correct count is zero, which makes the rule visible from their own work rather than from being told again. Practices 5 and 6 are field tasks with no key and both carry a what-most-people-find note.

teacherNotes.type: This is the largest unit in Level 1
teacherNotes.note: It opens the past, which is where most of what an adult wants to say about their own life lives. Cards 1 and 2 are one pattern in two halves and should not be separated across sessions. If a learner is short of time, Pattern 3 is the one to protect: it removes half the irregular-verb burden, and a learner who has it can survive with an incomplete list.

teacherNotes.type: Why twenty and not a hundred
teacherNotes.note: Reading 1 states the real size of the problem rather than the frightening one. The twenty chosen are the highest-frequency irregulars and several are already known passively. The pair drill in Speaking 2 exists because a pair is one item of memory and two isolated forms are two, and because said and heard are sound irregularities that silent reading does not teach.

teacherNotes.type: Did you went is the error to expect
teacherNotes.note: Marking the past twice is the dominant error and it survives long after the rule is understood, because both halves feel like they should agree. It is largely a speech error rather than a writing one, which is why Speaking 3 asks for eighteen recorded items and Practice 6 asks learners to notice themselves doing it in real conversation. Being told the rule once does not fix it; hearing yourself do it usually does.

teacherNotes.type: Why a report and a witness statement
teacherNotes.note: The two documents are the clearest available demonstration of hedged and unhedged register, and the comprehension turns on three things: the central event was not actually witnessed, the stated cause is supported only as an impression, and the witness contradicts themselves about timing without noticing. Reading 2 supplies the three questions that make those findings reachable, and they generalise well beyond incidents — two colleagues describing a meeting works the same way.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Writing 1 and Speaking 4 ask learners to recount a real day, and Practice 6 asks them to ask another person what happened to them: nothing personal about the learner or the other person should be collected, shared or entered into the app. Practice 6 asks only for the questions used and one thing learned, not for the other person's account, and that wording should stay.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say worked, lived and started correctly, and hear which ones have an extra syllable.
I can say went, saw, came and took without stopping to think.
I can ask did you go and say I didn't go, without putting the past on both verbs.
I can say two weeks ago and last week, and notice where two accounts of an event differ.

assignment.title: A day told, and two accounts compared
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record the story of one real day from your past, ten to fourteen sentences, using at least eight irregular verbs and three story adverbs — then listen back, count the past forms you got wrong, and record one further sentence naming them. Second, write full-sentence answers to the five questions in Writing 3 about the report and statement in Reading 3, and add the two questions you would ask the witness to resolve the contradiction about timing. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written answers
